subject: Copywriting
title: The Rise of HTML Email
description: A quick, practical guide to The Rise of HTML Email.

hook.text: In 1996, Hotmail launched free email. Suddenly every human had an inbox, and brands raced to fill it.

buildup.text: HTML emails replaced plain text in the late 1990s. Colors, images, and buttons made emails look like miniature websites.

discovery.text: Brands could now track opens and clicks. For the first time, email copy was measurable per-word, per-link.

twist.text: HTML emails broke constantly. Outlook, Gmail, and Yahoo all rendered differently. Copy had to survive broken layouts.

climax.text: The design arms race taught a lesson: a clear message in plain text often outperforms a beautiful but broken HTML email.

punchline.text: Beautiful emails break. Clear words work in every inbox.

quiz.question: What problem plagued HTML emails?
options: Different email clients rendered them differently

details.summary: HTML email replaced plain text in the late 1990s, allowing brands to include images, colors, buttons, and formatted layouts. While HTML enabled richer visual experiences, it also introduced rendering challenges — emails can look different across Gmail, Outlook, and Apple Mail, creating a unique...
details.whyItMatters: HTML email is the standard for modern marketing, but its rendering quirks demand specialized knowledge. Understanding its constraints helps writers and designers create emails that look good everywhere.
takeaways: HTML email enabled visual branding in the inbox for the first time
Email rendering varies significantly across major email clients
Table-based layouts remain necessary due to inconsistent CSS support

faq.question: Why do HTML emails look different in different email clients?
faq.answer: Unlike web browsers that follow shared standards, email clients like Outlook, Gmail, and Apple Mail each render HTML differently. Outlook uses Microsoft Word's rendering engine, which strips modern CSS. This forces email designers to use older HTML techniques like table-based layouts.

faq.question: Should marketing emails use HTML or plain text?
faq.answer: It depends on the goal. HTML enables branding and visual calls to action. Plain text feels more personal and often achieves higher reply rates. Many successful marketers use HTML for promotional campaigns and plain text for personal outreach and relationship building.
